phonemes.desc: Initial syllable with open [a], stressed in the anglicized citation form; the first consonant is a plain alveolar stop.
Unstressed medial syllable; the tapped or trilled quality of the original southeastern languages is usually flattened to an English approximant [ɹ] in citation.
Closed back rounded vowel [ʊ] followed by a bilabial nasal; the vowel is short and soft.
Final syllable with lateral [l] plus a short back rounded vowel; the name ends gently, without a final consonant cluster.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DARR-uh-MOO-lum' — four even syllables, stress on the first, with the soft 'oo' of 'book' in the third and fourth syllables.

kin.label: Dharug/Eora region
kin.form: Daramulum, the sky hero and son of Baiame recorded in the Sydney–Blue Mountains cultural area

kin.label: Euahlayi (Kamilaroi) tradition
kin.form: Baiame's son, sometimes named as the one-legged being who presides over initiation and the Law

pronunciation.note: The name is Tier 2 in the PuniCodex system: the ASCII string 'daramulum' already encodes the same phonemic material. The restoration capitalizes the initial letter to mark a proper name, but no stress mark, length mark, or distinctive letter is added.

domains.title: Sky Hero of the Bora
domains.subtitle: Initiation, Law, and the Emu in the Sky
domains.lead: Daramulum is the one-legged son of Baiame, the great creator and sky father of several Aboriginal nations in southeastern Australia. He moves between earth and sky as an enforcer and teacher of the Law, presiding over the bora initiation ground where boys become men. His body is sometimes described as emu-like or one-legged, linking him to the dark silhouette of the emu that stretches across the Milky Way — the 'Emu in the Sky' that Aboriginal astronomers have used for millennia to mark seasons and ceremonies.

cards.name: Sky Hero
cards.desc: Son of Baiame and a power of the upper world; his camp is said to lie in the sky, especially among the stars of the Milky Way.

cards.name: Keeper of the Bora
cards.desc: Guardian of the bora ring and the initiation ceremonies through which Law, identity, and adult responsibility are transmitted.

cards.name: Emu in the Sky
cards.desc: His one-legged form is identified with the dark emu traced in the Milky Way, a seasonal clock and sacred map.

cards.name: Son of Baiame
cards.desc: The principal male descendant of the creator-sky father, acting as his agent in teaching, judging, and protecting the Law.

symbols.name: Boomerang
symbols.meaning: Emblem of initiation, return, and the lawful exchange between earth and sky; also a weapon associated with Daramulum's authority.

symbols.name: Emu
symbols.meaning: His one-legged or emu-footed form; the dark emu in the Milky Way is read as his celestial body.

symbols.name: Bora ring
symbols.meaning: The sacred ground where initiation is performed and where Daramulum's presence is invoked.

symbols.name: Centre of the Milky Way
symbols.meaning: The camp or turning-place of Daramulum and Baiame in the sky; a focus of southeastern Aboriginal astronomy.

mythology.lead: Daramulum's mythology is preserved in the ceremonial life and oral traditions of the Dharug, Eora, and neighbouring nations of New South Wales. He is not a remote deity but an active guardian of social order: he descends for initiations, carries the boomerang of judgment, and lives in the sky as a permanent sign of the Law.

myths.title: The One-Legged Son of Baiame
myths.text: Daramulum is the son of Baiame, the creator and sky father. Accounts collected in the Sydney region describe him as a being of strange form — sometimes one-legged, sometimes with an emu's foot — who serves as his father's messenger and enforcer. His unusual body is not a deformity but a sign of his other-than-human nature and his connection to the emu, a bird that stands on one leg and that appears in the sky as a dark constellation.

myths.title: The Bora and the Law
myths.text: The bora is the initiation ground where boys are ritually introduced to the responsibilities of men. Daramulum is said to attend these ceremonies as guardian and witness; the bullroarer, a sacred instrument whose sound is heard from the bora ring, is sometimes identified with his voice or with the voice of Baiame speaking through him. To break the secrecy of the bora or to mock its procedures is to risk his anger.

myths.title: The Emu in the Sky
myths.text: In the dark spaces of the Milky Way, Aboriginal observers trace the body of an emu: the head in the Coalsack near the Southern Cross, the neck and body stretching through the Centaurus and Scorpius dust lanes, and the legs toward Ophiuchus. For some southeastern traditions this celestial emu is Daramulum himself, or his camp, or the sign by which he watches over the seasons. When the emu stands upright in the evening sky, it is time to collect emu eggs; when she sits, it is time for ceremony.

myths.title: The Sky Camp
myths.text: After performing his work on earth, Daramulum is said to have returned to a camp in the sky, near Baiame's own place. From there he continues to oversee initiations, to send rain and storms, and to keep the moral order of the world. The Milky Way is not merely decorative: it is the road, the river, and the camping ground of ancestral powers, with Daramulum's position marking one of its most important stations.

etymology.protoLanguage: Southeastern Australian Aboriginal language (unattested proto-form; recorded in colonial orthographies)
etymology.derivation: The name is recorded as meaning 'the one-legged' in nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnographic sources. The gloss probably refers to Daramulum's emu-like or single-legged form rather than to a literal anatomical description. The precise Aboriginal-language etymology is uncertain because the term reached English through several colonial spellings and language contact situations.
